prerequisites.check: Does rewriting a prompt change the model's stored weights?
prerequisites.answer: No. It changes the input for one request; the weights stay fixed.

prerequisites.meaning: The fraction of evaluated examples counted as correct.
prerequisites.check: If 16 of 20 labels are correct, what is the accuracy?

prerequisites.meaning: A structured text format for exchanging fields and values, including objects and lists.
prerequisites.answer: No. Code can read it, but its values can still be wrong.

diagrams.title: The prompt evaluation loop
diagrams.subtitle: Weights fixed
trace: The development ticket "I can't log into Moodle" has the known label IT_ACCESS.
few_shot adds the task, the five labels and five worked examples.
llm returns a short reply with greedy decoding and an eight-token cap.
label_scorer finds IT_ACCESS and compares it with the known label.
evaluate reports accuracy, invalid replies and average output tokens for 20 messages.
diagrams.explanation: A labelled message goes into a prompt function, which returns chat messages. The model generates a reply with fixed settings: greedy decoding and a small token cap. A scorer reads the reply, finds a recognised label and compares it with the known answer. The evaluate function repeats this for every development message and summarises accuracy, invalid replies, average output tokens and seconds. Only the prompt changes between runs, so differences come from the prompt. Reading the failed replies explains what the number cannot: a wrong team, an invalid sentence or a genuinely ambiguous message.
diagrams.check_answer: No. Only the prompt changes between runs; the model weights stay fixed.
diagrams.notes:
In short: The evaluation loop holds the model fixed, changes one prompt, and scores every reply against a known answer.

Explain: A development set is a small labelled collection used while revising prompts. A prompt function turns one message into chat messages. The model generates a short reply with fixed settings. A scorer turns that reply into a number and a note. The harness averages scores and records output tokens.

Example: The ticket "I can't log into Moodle" has the label IT_ACCESS. The few-shot prompt adds five worked examples. A reply of "IT_ACCESS" scores 1; "IT ACCESS" also counts. Across 20 messages, 17 correct gives 85%. A driving-test route is an analogy; one route for every candidate makes scores comparable. Unlike a test route, a prompt can be tuned to fit these particular messages.

Ask: Which part changes between two runs of the loop?

Answer: Only the prompt function; the model, settings, messages and scorer stay fixed.

Watch out: Reading the wrong replies matters as much as the accuracy number.

diagrams.insert_before_title: Structured outputs: a schema as a contract
diagrams.title: JSON extraction with a check
diagrams.subtitle: Shape, then facts
trace: Aoife's email supplies a name, an eight-digit ID, an extension request and a date.
The prompt asks for those four fields, with null when no date is present.
Malformed JSON or a seven-digit ID triggers the error branch.
The error message goes back to the model once; a second failure returns None.
A valid object is then compared field by field with the gold values.
diagrams.explanation: Structured extraction asks the model for a JSON object with named fields. Parsing turns the reply text into a Python dictionary, and the Request schema checks each field: a name, an eight-digit student ID, one of three request types and an ISO date or null. When parsing or validation fails, the error message goes back to the model once and the retry is checked again. A valid object is not yet a correct one: each field must still be compared with the facts in the source email.
diagrams.check_answer: Yes. A wrong eight-digit ID passes the format check; only comparison with the email reveals it.
diagrams.notes:
In short: Structured extraction checks the shape of the reply first and the facts second.

Explain: A schema lists required fields, their types and allowed values. Parsing turns JSON text into a Python dictionary. Validation checks each field against the schema rules. A retry sends the error back to the model once. Correctness compares each valid field with the source email.

Example: Aoife's email gives the ID 23145678 and the date 14 March 2027. A reply containing 2314567 fails the eight-digit rule, so the error goes back once. A reply containing 23145687 passes validation but is wrong. A paper form with labelled boxes is an analogy; the boxes force the format, but cannot check what is written in them.

Ask: Can a wrong eight-digit student ID pass validation?

Answer: Yes. The format rule passes; only comparing with the email reveals the wrong value.

Watch out: Count valid outputs and correct outputs separately, because they measure different things.

diagrams.title: Choose on development; report on held-out
diagrams.subtitle: Part 1
trace: The 40 synthetic tickets split into 20 development and 20 held-out messages, four per team each.
Zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot and role + few-shot prompts run on the development messages.
The highest accuracy, with fewer output tokens as the tie-break, selects one prompt.
Only that prompt runs once on the held-out messages.
The evidence table reports both accuracies with the model and settings.
diagrams.explanation: Part 1 compares four prompts on 20 development messages, where you may read errors and revise. The best development prompt is then run once on 20 held-out messages that played no part in the choice. The held-out accuracy is the fairer estimate for new messages, because choosing a prompt on the same messages you report tends to overstate its accuracy. With 20 messages, one item moves accuracy by five percentage points, so small differences need cautious wording.
diagrams.check_answer: The prompt was chosen on the development messages, so their score overstates accuracy on new messages.
diagrams.notes:
In short: The lab chooses a prompt on development messages and reports it once on held-out messages.

Explain: The 40 synthetic tickets are split into two halves of 20. Four prompts run on the development half. The best accuracy, with fewer tokens as a tie-break, picks the prompt. The chosen prompt then runs once on the held-out half. Both accuracies go into the evidence table.

Example: Suppose few-shot scores 85% on development and 75% on held-out messages. The ten-point drop is two messages out of 20. It suggests part of the development gain fitted those particular messages. Practising on past exam papers and then sitting a new paper is an analogy; only the new paper shows what transfers.

Ask: Why not report the development score as the final result?

Answer: The prompt was chosen on those messages, so their score overstates accuracy on new messages.

Watch out: Never revise the prompt after reading held-out errors, or that set stops being held out.

diagrams.title: Improve a prompt using evidence
diagrams.subtitle: Weights fixed
trace: Suppose prompt A gets 16 of 20 development labels right and prompt B gets 17.
Accuracy changes from 80% to 85%; one message produces the gain.
Read that message and any newly wrong ones before choosing B.
Run the chosen prompt once on held-out messages before claiming an improvement.
diagrams.explanation: Prompt development changes one component at a time, such as the examples or the role, and runs both versions with the same model, messages and settings. Comparing the two summaries shows the net change in accuracy, but reading the items that changed shows why: a revision can fix two messages and break one. Model weights never change in this loop. When a prompt has been chosen, a single run on held-out messages checks whether the gain transfers.
diagrams.check_answer: No. Only the prompt changed; one more message was answered correctly.
diagrams.notes:
In short: Prompt development compares two prompt versions on the same development messages, then reads the items that changed.

Explain: Prompts A and B differ in one component only. Both run with the same model, messages and settings. The comparison shows which messages changed from wrong to right, and back. A held-out set gives one final check after choosing. Model weights never change in this loop.

Example: Prompt A gets 16 of 20 development labels right; prompt B gets 17. Accuracy rises from 80% to 85%, which is one message. Suppose B fixes two messages but breaks one: the net gain is still one. Editing an essay against a fixed marking guide is an analogy; you change the text, not the marker.

Ask: Did the rise from 80% to 85% change any model weights?

Answer: No. Only the prompt changed; one more message was answered correctly.

Watch out: A one-message gain on 20 examples is weak evidence; confirm it on held-out messages.

diagrams.title: Route one new message
diagrams.subtitle: Chosen prompt
trace: New message: "I cannot sign in to Moodle."
The prompt lists IT_ACCESS and the other permitted teams.
The model replies "IT_ACCESS".
The scorer recognises exactly one label; a reply naming two teams is counted as invalid.
diagrams.explanation: Inference uses the fixed model and the chosen prompt to answer one new message. The prompt lists the five allowed teams with one example each, generation stops after at most eight new tokens, and the scorer accepts a reply only when it names exactly one label. A recognised label is a valid routing decision, but it can still be the wrong team; only comparison with a known label, or human review in a real service, shows whether it is correct.
diagrams.check_answer: Yes. Parsing checks the form; only the known label shows whether the team is correct.
diagrams.notes:
In short: Inference applies the chosen prompt to one new message and turns the reply into one team label.

Explain: Inference means using fixed weights to answer a new input. The prompt lists the five allowed teams and five examples. Generation stops after at most eight new tokens. The scorer accepts a reply naming exactly one label. A reply naming two teams counts as invalid.

Example: "I cannot sign in to Moodle" goes into the few-shot prompt. The model replies "IT_ACCESS", which the scorer recognises. A reply of "IT_ACCESS or LIBRARY" would be invalid. A postal sorting machine is an analogy; it reads a code and picks one bin. Unlike the machine, the model can pick a valid but wrong bin.

Ask: Can a recognised label still be wrong?

Answer: Yes. Parsing checks the form; only the known label shows whether the team is correct.

Watch out: Never count a reply as correct because the right team appears among several named teams.

glossary.meaning: A prompt describing the task without including worked input/output examples.
A prompt containing several examples of the desired input/output behaviour.
Code that runs examples, scores outputs and collects comparable measures.
A specification of output fields, types and allowed values.
Instructions inside supplied content that attempt to redirect the model's task.
A judge's preference for an answer's placement rather than its quality.
A reference answer or observation used to check a model output.
A unit processed or generated by a model; a text token can be a word, word part or character.

pitfalls: A valid JSON object can contain incorrect facts or a calendar-impossible date that matches the current pattern check.
Adding examples to a prompt supplies context rather than performing fine-tuning.
A tiny accuracy gain, a keyword attack detector or invalid judge replies can create misleading conclusions.

code_walkthrough.inspect: Read outputs that mention zero, one or multiple permitted labels.

code_walkthrough.inspect: Observe missing parses and ties before interpreting the vote.

recap.title: What we learned: prompts and evidence
recap.question: Valid JSON proves facts?
recap.notes:
In short: Prompting changes the input, not the model, so every claimed improvement needs a fair, measured comparison.

Explain: A clear brief states rules, sources, examples, task and format. Step-by-step prompts can help multi-step problems but cost tokens. A schema checks structure; a gold comparison checks facts. Held-out messages give the fairer final estimate. Injected instructions are untrusted data, so permissions belong in code.

Example: On 20 messages, one changed answer moves accuracy by five percentage points. A JSON reply with a well-formed but wrong ID still passes the schema. A judge that picks A in both orders is following position, not quality.

Ask: What evidence would convince you that a prompt revision helped?

Answer: A gain on the same development messages, confirmed once on held-out messages, with costs and errors reported.

Watch out: Do not mix the stored GPU results with your own CPU run without naming the model and settings.

vocabulary_notes:
In short: Prompts, accuracy and JSON are the three ideas needed to read every table in today's lab.

Explain: A prompt is the input text for one request. Changing it changes the request, not the stored weights. Accuracy is correct items divided by all scored items. JSON is a text format with named fields that code can read. Valid JSON can still contain wrong values.

Example: Suppose a prompt routes 16 of 20 development messages correctly. Its accuracy is 16 ÷ 20 = 0.8, or 80%. One more correct message gives 85%, so one item moves the score by five percentage points. A JSON reply such as {"student_id": "23145678"} parses correctly even when the email gave a different number.

Ask: If 17 of 20 messages are correct, what is the accuracy?

Answer: 85%, because 17 ÷ 20 = 0.85.

Watch out: On a small development set every single item counts, so do not over-read a five-point change.
